newsitem.title: USA: Inland says not hurt by GM strike.
newsitem.headline: Inland says not hurt by GM strike.

text.p: Inland Steel Industries Inc has not slowed its shipments to General Motors Corp in the face of a strike at the automaker but shipments will be affected if the strike drags on, Inland Steel officials said Tuesday.

General Motors is the single largest customer of U.S. steelmakers. "(The strike) hasn't had an adverse effect on us at this point," Jay Gratz, Inland Steel's chief financial officer, told reporters on a conference call following the company's release of third-quarter earnings.
"Clearly, if it goes on for a very long period of time (shipments will be hurt."), he added.
A strike by 26,000 members of the Canadian Autoworkers union that has halted production in Canada has begun idling General Motors' plants in the United States and Mexico.
As of Monday, the automaker had idled 5,900 workers in Mexico and the United States.
Inland Steel, the nation's fifth-largest integrated steelmaker, posted third-quarter earnings of $0.13 per share, compared with $0.33 per share a year earlier.

This year's quarterly results include an $8.8 million after-tax charge for the early retirement of company bonds. Excluding the charge, earnings were $0.31 per share, above Wall Street's consensus estimate of $0.27 per share.

Revenues fell slightly this year to $1.12 billion from $1.13 billion last year. Operating profit per ton, a measure of a steel company's performance, fell to $21 per ton this year from $33 per ton last year.
Industry analysts are expecting steel companies to post lower profits this year because steel prices have fallen from last year's levels.
Gratz said Inland Steel's order book is "fairly strong" and large markets including the automotive and appliance industries are strong.
